Q: Why can't I access remote Jupyter Notebook server? A:

I can enter the bash of the computer, just not the Jupyter Notebook with jupyter notebook --no-browser --port=8889 --ip=0.0.0.0, as in the question.

Firefox shows something like:

My own translation:

Connection failed
Firefox cannot build a connection with server 127.0.0.1:8891.

German:

Verbindung fehlgeschlagen
Firefox kann keine Verbindung zu dem Server unter 127.0.0.1:8891 aufbauen.

Wait

I often have this problem when working with a remote computer in an ssh tunnel and my own laptop crashes or loses the connection while the remote server still runs the process so that I have to wait until the remote computer closes the orphaned process by itself after some 10 to 15 minutes.

Thus, the first answer to this question is, that you can wait for 15 minutes, and then you might be lucky that everything works again. Or you wait for an hour or a day, that depends on the settings how orphaned processes are kept alive on the remote server.

Kill

Kill chosen pid:s

But I do not want to wait so long. First, I check whether I can enter the Jupyter Notebook from another laptop. I still see the error in I check the running processes with ps on the ssh-connected remote computer and find just bash and ps. Those were just the two processes that I was in, they should not be the problem.

You might still find pid:s with ps that you might want to kill, for example for pid 4711:

kill -SIGTERM 4711

You should always try it with -SIGTERM at first since that is the normal closing, not a forced closing.

But I cannot do this since my bash pid is the pid that I am in, and I do not see anything else that might run and block.

Kill all processes that you are allowed to (the main trick!)

But I thought, why not give it a chance and stop all processes that I am allowed to stop. Perhaps, ps does not show all of the pids.

Run:

kill -SIGTERM -1

or:

kill -15 -1

Out:

$ kill -SIGTERM -1
Connection to localhost closed by remote host.
Connection to localhost closed.

Both are the same, run kill -l for the list of the parameters. This will kill all processes that you are allowed to and throws you out of the bash.

See kill - Wiki Ubuntu Users.

And right after doing so, I can enter the Jupyter Notebook server again.

I had this error again, and kill -SIGTERM -1 worked again.

Q: intptr_t and size_t on 32/64 bit platform A:

When to use intptr_t, size_t data type?

Roughly speaking:
size_t is for an object's size and array indexing.
(u)intptr_t are for an object's address.

size_t is always available - it is part of the C language. It is some unsigned type useful for indexing arrays and performing size calculations. It is the best width integer for indexing as it is never too narrow nor excessively wide.

Code can use printf("%zu\n", some_size_t); to print.

(u)intptr_t are optionally yet commonly implemented. They are part of the C standard library. They are integer types capable of round-tripping object pointers object * --> void * --> intptr_t --> void * --> object * with a resultant pointer that equates to the original.

Code can use printf( "%" PRIdPTR "\n", some_intptr_t); to print.

With many C implementations, these types are the same size (still use matching specifier when printing/scanning). Yet implementations exist where the address is wider than the size. I know of no implementation were the reverse is true.

Can we use %z instead of PRIdPTR when trying to print intptr_t?

This does not make for portable code. Aside from the difference in sign-ness, it is reasonable to encounter implementations that differ in integer width, with intptr_t likely be wider or as wide as size_t.

[Further: Function pointers]

"use intptr_t if you want to store a pointer in an integral type." is reasonable for object pointers and void *. Function pointers may differ in size (common enough in 2025) and encoding than object pointers. Converting function pointers to void * or to (u)intptr_t may lose information, even on a "64 bit platform". Unfortunately C lacks a defined integer type for such conversions.

Pre C23: Function pointers might fit in (u)intmax_t or some implementation specified type like uint128.

With C23 and _BitInt integers, I suspect function pointer conversion to/from a sufficiently wide integer may be possible - yet this still holds a number of restrictions like BITINT_MAXWIDTH,. If wanting to explore area, here be dragons.

For highly portable code, consider a union of a function pointer and unsigned char b[sizeof(int (*)(int))] or the like (e.g. cast) and treat the function pointer as a blob of binary data in which to print.
